newsitem.title: USA: Muni yields hit richest levels in over two years.
newsitem.headline: Muni yields hit richest levels in over two years.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond yields dipped below 80 percent as a percentage of U.S. Treasuries for the first time in more than two years on Tuesday, a level that in the past has signaled potential trouble, according to Delphis Hanover Corp.
But whether current ratios will drive municipals into a traditional retreat--or constitute just a marker on the road to new territory--has been the subject of debate among market participants.

"I think we are in a different game right now," Reid Smith, a principal and senior portfolio manager at the Vanguard Group. "Technically, there is nothing out there to cause a cheapening of the ratios."
Austin Tobin, president of Connecticut-based Delphis Hanover Corp, said the 80 percent mark has been a key barometer for municipals.
Since 1986, anytime municipals have remained below 80 percent of Treasury yields for roughly a week, a noticeable downward adjustment has ensued, Tobin said.

Delphis Hanover figures for Tuesday show 30-year, triple-A municipal bond yields at 79.7 percent of 30-year Treasuries, setting a new 52-week low ratio. The previous low of 80.2 percent was established on May 23.

The last time municipals dipped below 80 percent of Treasuries was more two years ago, on March 7, 1995, when the ratio hit 78.6 percent, Delphis figures show. The highest ratio recorded in the past 52 weeks was 86.2 percent, set on November 12, 1996.

In Smith Barney Inc's most recent Credit Market Comment, a graph of Smith Barney's Revenue Bond Index as a percentage of 30-year Treasuries from August 1993 to through last week showed "municipal yields are now down to the yield ratio which has been a powerful 'resistance point' during previous cycles."
But despite what appear to be traditionally rich levels, the report by George Friedlander and Bart Mosley said it remains unclear whether the municipal market has hit a wall or still has room to run.
"The question then is whether it can stay up at these high altitudes--are we at a 'base camp' or the peak of a mountain?," the report said.
Municipals have grown rich to U.S. for several reasons, the Smith Barney report said. Supply has been moderate and dealer inventory has been "very light."
Meanwhile, demand from certain institutional buyers has been strong.
Property and casualty companies have exhibited a "seemingly endless appetitite" for municipals, despite their increasingly rich relationship to governments.
In addition, demand from retail investors has remained "surprisingly strong," due likely in part to money that traditionally flows back to muni investors in June and July, the report said.
But while others may describe municipals as rich to Treasuries, Vanguard's Reid Smith disagrees.
"We think that they are on the rich side of their fair range," he said. "We don't view them as rich at this point."
Though he acknowledged that municipal yields have come a long way since last November, Smith said the improvement should not worry investors.

"The MOB has performed extremely well since the fourth quarter of '96," the portfolio manager said. "And we don't see any reason that someone should be wary of where munis are going right now relative to taxables. It could, in our estimation, get richer."

Supply remains thin, and demand remains brisk heading into the June and July re-investment period, Smith said. Also notable was that munis were able to maintain such low yield ratios to Treasuries during April and May.

"Most of the time we do see a cheapening up in April and May because of supply," he said. "What's happened is there has been strong buying demand in munis during the heavy supply period in April and May. Consequently, the ratios stayed unchanged."
((--Kathie O'Donnell, 212-859-1655))
